source: CoreGuard Quilla Cyber Codex — defensive summaries of publicly documented mobile attack methods (OWASP MASTG/WSTG orientation, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile, vendor advisories). Not exploit code.
license_note: Educational paraphrase for on-device defense. See references.

entries.title: Accessibility / overlay phishing (modern mobile)
entries.summary: Malware abuses Accessibility or draw-over-apps to steal credentials via fake screens.
entries.body: Contemporary Android banking trojans and stalkerware often request Accessibility Services, then paint convincing login overlays over legitimate apps or system dialogs. Victims type credentials into the overlay; the implant exfiltrates them. Related tricks include notification listeners, clipboard scrape, and session cookie theft from WebViews. This is a social-engineering + privilege abuse pattern, not a kernel exploit.
entries.defense: Deny Accessibility to untrusted apps. Review draw-over-other-apps permission. Prefer biometric/OS autofill. Run Nemesis after installing new apps. Enable Privacy Shield on hostile networks. Quilla will not help build overlays.

entries.title: Sideloaded dropper / trojanized APK supply chain
entries.summary: Attackers distribute modified APKs outside Play with nested payloads.
entries.body: Operators ship 'modded' or 'cracked' APKs, SMS/Telegram droppers, or lookalike apps that unpack a second-stage payload after install. Techniques include encrypted asset DEX, dynamic code loading, and delayed C2 beacons to evade first-run scanners. Authorized pentests enumerate sideload paths under ROE; criminals use the same paths without consent.
entries.defense: Install only from trusted stores. Disable unknown sources. Scan with Nemesis after any sideload. Uninstall apps you do not recognize. Quilla refuses help packaging malware.

entries.title: Deep link / Intent redirection abuse
entries.summary: Crafted links or Intents coerce apps into unsafe actions.
entries.body: Misconfigured exported Activities, custom URL schemes, and App Links can be hijacked so a malicious app or phishing page opens a victim app into an attacker-controlled WebView, bypasses auth screens, or leaks tokens. Mobile pentests map exported components; defenders lock exports, validate deep-link origins, and disable JavaScript bridges where unnecessary.
entries.defense: Keep apps updated. Avoid opening unexpected links. Prefer verified App Links. Developers: mark components non-exported, validate intents, and avoid trusting WebView content. Quilla teaches defense, not exploit PoCs.

entries.title: Commercial spyware & zero-click messaging paths (defender view)
entries.summary: High-end spyware may exploit messaging stacks without user taps; detection leans on IOCs and forensics.
entries.body: Public Amnesty / MVT reporting documents mercenary spyware that can compromise phones via messaging or zero-click paths. Non-rooted on-device scanners cannot guarantee absence of such implants, but IOC matching (domains, processes, packages, paths) and timeline forensics raise signal. Clean scans are reassuring, not absolute.
entries.defense: Keep OS patched. Prefer latest messaging apps. Use Nemesis + Amnesty/MVT IOC refresh (Premium signatures). Enable Shield. High-risk users: consider device replacement after confirmed compromise. Quilla correlates public IOCs — it does not sell or teach spyware ops.

entries.title: RASP / anti-tamper bypass attempts (awareness)
entries.summary: Attackers and authorized testers probe for Frida, Magisk, and debugger hooks.
entries.body: Dynamic instrumentation (Frida, Xposed-class frameworks), Magisk hide, and debugger attach are used both by legitimate mobile pentesters (with written ROE) and by malware authors to defeat certificate pinning, root detection, or in-app RASP. Signals include unexpected tracers, modified libc, and injected libraries.
entries.defense: CoreGuard's native tamper checks and RASP telemetry raise these signals for correlation. On a personal device: avoid rooting, avoid unknown Magisk modules, and treat sudden integrity failures as reason to rescan. Quilla will not coach bypassing protections on third-party apps.

entries.title: DNS tunneling & malicious domain C2
entries.summary: Implants resolve or tunnel through DNS to reach command infrastructure.
entries.body: Many mobile implants use short-lived domains, DGA-like names, or DNS queries as a covert channel. Domain blocklists (including Amnesty/MVT-style IOCs) can NXDOMAIN known C2 names via a local VPN DNS filter. Hardcoded IPs bypass DNS filters — a documented limitation.
entries.defense: Keep Privacy Shield on when you need DNS IOC sinkholing. Combine with Nemesis package/process scans. Prefer trusted networks. Quilla correlates Shield blocks against STIX IOCs.

entries.title: OWASP MASTG orientation for authorized mobile tests
entries.summary: MASTG structures authorized Android/iOS testing; always under written ROE.
entries.body: The OWASP Mobile Application Security Testing Guide organizes static/dynamic tests for storage, crypto, auth, network, platform interaction, code quality, and resiliency. Professional testers map findings to MASVS controls and deliver remediation-focused reports. Unauthorized testing is illegal.
entries.defense: Use MASTG as a checklist to harden your own apps and devices. Ask Quilla about MASVS categories. Never use Quilla to attack systems you do not own or lack permission to test.

entries.title: WSTG API abuse patterns that hit mobile backends
entries.summary: Mobile apps often fail open at the API — IDOR/BOLA, weak tokens, over-sharing.
entries.body: Even a polished APK can talk to APIs with broken object-level authorization, long-lived tokens in logs, or excessive data in responses. OWASP WSTG and API Security Top 10 catalog these for authorized assessments. Defenders rotate tokens, enforce server-side authz, and minimize client trust.
entries.defense: As a user: prefer apps with modern auth, enable MFA on accounts the app touches, and revoke sessions after device loss. Developers: server-side checks, short-lived tokens, certificate pinning with backup pins. Quilla explains patterns — not exploit scripts against live targets.
